claim: STAT1 KO mice spontaneously developed an inflammatory disease marked by myeloid hyperplasia and splenic accumulation of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: We report that STAT1 KO mice spontaneously developed an inflammatory disease marked by myeloid hyperplasia and splenic accumulation of hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: STAT1 KO mice developed inflammatory bowel disease.
source: Moreover, these animals developed inflammatory bowel disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by histological and clinical data in the results section.

claim: STAT1 KO mice exhibited a profound dysbiosis in gut bacteria.
source: Profiling gut bacteria revealed a profound dysbiosis in the absence of tonic IFN signaling, which triggered expansion of TH17 cells and loss of splenic Treg cells.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data showing altered microbiome composition.

claim: Dysbiosis in STAT1 KO mice triggered expansion of TH17 cells.
source: Profiling gut bacteria revealed a profound dysbiosis in the absence of tonic IFN signaling, which triggered expansion of TH17 cells and loss of splenic Treg cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased IL-17A-producing CD4+ T cells.

claim: Dysbiosis in STAT1 KO mice caused loss of splenic Treg cells.
source: Profiling gut bacteria revealed a profound dysbiosis in the absence of tonic IFN signaling, which triggered expansion of TH17 cells and loss of splenic Treg cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing virtually absent peripheral Treg cells in STAT1 KO spleens.

claim: Reduction of bacterial load by antibiotic treatment averted the TH17 bias in STAT1 KO mice.
source: Reduction of bacterial load by antibiotic treatment averted the TH17 bias and blocking IL17 signaling prevented myeloid expansion and splenic stem cell accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing decreased IL-17+ CD4+ T cells after antibiotic treatment.

claim: Blocking IL-17 signaling prevented myeloid expansion in STAT1 KO mice.
source: Reduction of bacterial load by antibiotic treatment averted the TH17 bias and blocking IL17 signaling prevented myeloid expansion and splenic stem cell accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by data from STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice showing normalized blood parameters.

claim: Blocking IL-17 signaling prevented splenic stem cell accumulation in STAT1 KO mice.
source: Reduction of bacterial load by antibiotic treatment averted the TH17 bias and blocking IL17 signaling prevented myeloid expansion and splenic stem cell accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by data from STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice showing no increase in splenic HSCs.

claim: Tonic IFNs regulate gut microbial ecology.
source: Thus, tonic IFNs regulate gut microbial ecology, which is crucial for maintaining physiologic immune homeostasis and preventing inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis showing dysbiosis in mice lacking IFN signaling.

claim: Gut microbial ecology regulated by tonic IFNs is crucial for maintaining physiologic immune homeostasis.
source: Thus, tonic IFNs regulate gut microbial ecology, which is crucial for maintaining physiologic immune homeostasis and preventing inflammation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dysbiosis leads to inflammatory disease in STAT1 KO mice.

claim: Gut microbial ecology regulated by tonic IFNs is crucial for preventing inflammation.
source: Thus, tonic IFNs regulate gut microbial ecology, which is crucial for maintaining physiologic immune homeostasis and preventing inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by the development of inflammatory disease in STAT1 KO mice with dysbiosis.

claim: STAT1 KO spleens were 5-10 times larger than wild-type littermates.
source: STAT1 KO spleens were found to average 5–10 times larger than their wild-type (WT) littermates (Figure 1A) in absence of any notable infection.
evidence: This is supported by spleen weight measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Normal splenic architecture of STAT1 KO animals was disrupted with prominent signs of extramedullary hematopoiesis.
source: Moreover, the normal splenic architecture of STAT1 KO animals was disrupted, with prominent signs of extramedullary hematopoiesis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of total white blood cells was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO mice compared to WT (p=0.000007).
source: The number of total white blood cells (WBC, p=0.000007), as well as neutrophil (p=0.000034) and monocyte subsets (p=0.000029), was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO mice compared to WT (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by blood count data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The number of neutrophils was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO mice compared to WT (p=0.000034).
source: The number of total white blood cells (WBC, p=0.000007), as well as neutrophil (p=0.000034) and monocyte subsets (p=0.000029), was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO mice compared to WT (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by blood count data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The number of monocytes was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO mice compared to WT (p=0.000029).
source: The number of total white blood cells (WBC, p=0.000007), as well as neutrophil (p=0.000034) and monocyte subsets (p=0.000029), was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO mice compared to WT (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by blood count data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The percentage of neutrophils increased from an average of 7% in WT animals to about 50% of total blood cells in STAT1-deficient mice.
source: The percentage of neutrophils increased from an average of 7% in WT animals to about 50% of total blood cells in STAT1-deficient mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: STAT1 KO blood showed a reduced percentage of B lymphocytes compared to WT littermates.
source: Conversely, STAT1 KO blood showed a reduced percentage of B lymphocytes and NK cells when compared to WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: STAT1 KO blood showed a reduced percentage of NK cells compared to WT littermates.
source: Conversely, STAT1 KO blood showed a reduced percentage of B lymphocytes and NK cells when compared to WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A notable shift from naïve and central memory to effector T cells was observed for both CD4+ and CD8+ populations in STAT1 KO blood.
source: Interestingly, although the percentage of T cells did not change, a notable shift from naïve and central memory to effector T cells was observed for both CD4+ and CD8+ populations (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The total number of monocytes and neutrophils was approximately 100-fold higher in the KO spleen compared to WT.
source: Notably, because of the greatly increased cellularity of STAT1 KO spleens, the total number of monocytes and neutrophils was approximately 100-fold higher in the KO spleen compared to WT (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: STAT1 KO spleens contained close to 10 times more CD4+ effector T cells compared to WT spleens (p=0.00023).
source: Likewise, despite the differences in the percentage of effector T cells not being statistically significant (p=0.28 for CD4; p=0.36 for CD8), STAT1 KO spleens contained close to 10 times more CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells as compared to WT spleens, and these quantitative differences were highly statistically significant (Figure 1E, F, p=0.00023 for CD4; p=0.0058 for CD8).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: STAT1 KO spleens contained close to 10 times more CD8+ effector T cells compared to WT spleens (p=0.0058).
source: Likewise, despite the differences in the percentage of effector T cells not being statistically significant (p=0.28 for CD4; p=0.36 for CD8), STAT1 KO spleens contained close to 10 times more CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells as compared to WT spleens, and these quantitative differences were highly statistically significant (Figure 1E, F, p=0.00023 for CD4; p=0.0058 for CD8).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Analysis of progenitor populations in the bone marrow showed a significant increased percentage of GMP in STAT1 KO compared to WT (p=0.0009).
source: Analysis of progenitor populations in the bone marrow showed altered progenitor population ratios, with a significant increased percentage of GMP (p=0.0009) and decreased percentage of MEP in STAT1 KO compared to WT (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Analysis of progenitor populations in the bone marrow showed a decreased percentage of MEP in STAT1 KO compared to WT.
source: Analysis of progenitor populations in the bone marrow showed altered progenitor population ratios, with a significant increased percentage of GMP (p=0.0009) and decreased percentage of MEP in STAT1 KO compared to WT (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: An increased percentage and number of MEP was observed in the spleens of STAT1 KO mice, consistent with the presence of extramedullary hematopoiesis.
source: In contrast, we observed an increased percentage and number of MEP in the spleens of STAT1 KO mice, consistent with the presence of extramedullary hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and is consistent with histological findings.

claim: Phenotypic hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), defined as Lin−Sca1+c-Kit+CD150hiCD48low, were significantly expanded in STAT1-deficient spleens (p=0.00006).
source: More strikingly, phenotypic hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), defined as Lin−Sca1+c-Kit+CD150hiCD48low, which are very low in WT spleen, were significantly expanded in STAT1-deficient spleens (Figure 1H,I, p=0.00006).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: STAT1-deficient splenic progenitors showed much higher plating efficiency compared to WT.
source: In contrast, STAT1-deficient splenic progenitors showed much higher plating efficiency compared to WT, as well as greatly enhanced replating capacity.
evidence: This is supported by colony forming unit assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: STAT1-deficient splenic progenitors showed greatly enhanced replating capacity.
source: In contrast, STAT1-deficient splenic progenitors showed much higher plating efficiency compared to WT, as well as greatly enhanced replating capacity.
evidence: This is supported by colony forming unit assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: STAT1-deficient splenic progenitors still gave rise to a significant number of colonies after four sequential passages in methylcellulose.
source: Indeed, STAT1-deficient splenic progenitors still gave rise to a significant number of colonies after four sequential passages in methylcellulose (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by colony forming unit assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: STAT1-deficient spleens host a large population of self-renewing progenitors that is not normally found in WT animals.
source: This result provides evidence that STAT1-deficient spleens host a large population of self-renewing progenitors that is not normally found in WT animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced replating capacity observed in colony forming assays.

claim: WT splenic cells were not capable of thriving in irradiated hosts, with the few transplanted animals that survived showing the absence of donor-derived cells.
source: WT splenic cells were not capable of thriving in irradiated hosts, with the few transplanted animals that survived showing the absence of donor-derived cells (Figure 2C), indicative of the limited presence of HSCs in this organ under normal conditions (Morita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2C and cited literature.

claim: STAT1-deficient splenic cells reconstituted the host hematopoietic system as efficiently as WT or STAT1 KO BM, with a median reconstitution of over 80% donor-derived cells.
source: In contrast, STAT1-deficient splenic cells reconstituted the host hematopoietic system as efficiently as WT or STAT1 KO BM, with a median reconstitution of over 80 % donor-derived cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neither bone marrow nor spleen cells isolated from primary reconstituted animals that had received STAT1 KO bone marrow were capable of complementing secondary transplanted recipients, suggesting that STAT1 KO bone marrow was deficient in LT-HSCs.
source: Results from the secondary transplantation experiments showed even greater differences between WT and KO cells. Neither bone marrow nor spleen cells isolated from primary reconstituted animals that had received STAT1 KO bone marrow were capable of complementing secondary transplanted recipients, suggesting that STAT1 KO bone marrow was deficient in LT-HSCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by secondary transplantation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Bone marrow cells from primary animals reconstituted with STAT1 KO spleen cells had a reconstituting capacity indistinguishable (p=0.43) from animals initially reconstituted with WT bone marrow.
source: In marked contrast, bone marrow cells from primary animals reconstituted with STAT1 KO spleen cells had a reconstituting capacity indistinguishable (p=0.43) from animals initially reconstituted with WT bone marrow (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by secondary transplantation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fully functional pluripotent LT-HSCs reside in STAT1-deficient spleens.
source: These results strongly suggest that fully functional pluripotent LT-HSCs reside in STAT1-deficient spleens, that these cells, albeit residing in the spleen of STAT1-deficient animals, home to the BM following engraftment of WT animals, and that STAT1 KO BM is either depleted of LT-HSCs or these cells are functionally deficient.
evidence: This is inferred from transplantation experiments showing long-term reconstitution capacity.

claim: LT-HSCs from STAT1-deficient spleens home to the BM following engraftment of WT animals.
source: These results strongly suggest that fully functional pluripotent LT-HSCs reside in STAT1-deficient spleens, that these cells, albeit residing in the spleen of STAT1-deficient animals, home to the BM following engraftment of WT animals, and that STAT1 KO BM is either depleted of LT-HSCs or these cells are functionally deficient.
evidence: This is inferred from transplantation experiments showing reconstitution from splenic cells.

claim: STAT1 KO BM is either depleted of LT-HSCs or these cells are functionally deficient.
source: These results strongly suggest that fully functional pluripotent LT-HSCs reside in STAT1-deficient spleens, that these cells, albeit residing in the spleen of STAT1-deficient animals, home to the BM following engraftment of WT animals, and that STAT1 KO BM is either depleted of LT-HSCs or these cells are functionally deficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of STAT1 KO BM to reconstitute secondary recipients.

claim: No myeloid expansion or splenomegaly was detected in animals transplanted with STAT1 KO bone marrow or spleen.
source: Of note, no myeloid expansion or splenomegaly was detected in animals transplanted with STAT1 KO bone marrow or spleen, suggesting that loss of STAT1 solely in hematopoietic cells is not sufficient to cause the myeloproliferative disease observed in STAT1 KO mice.
evidence: This is an observation from transplantation experiments.

claim: Loss of STAT1 solely in hematopoietic cells is not sufficient to cause the myeloproliferative disease observed in STAT1 KO mice.
source: Of note, no myeloid expansion or splenomegaly was detected in animals transplanted with STAT1 KO bone marrow or spleen, suggesting that loss of STAT1 solely in hematopoietic cells is not sufficient to cause the myeloproliferative disease observed in STAT1 KO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of disease in transplanted animals.

claim: STAT1 KO mice died significantly faster than WT following weekly injections of 5-FU (p=0.01).
source: Following weekly injections of 5-FU, we documented that STAT1 KO mice died significantly faster than WT (p=0.01), and also faster than mice lacking both IFNAR and IFNGR (ARGR DKO) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: STAT1 KO mice died faster than ARGR DKO mice following weekly injections of 5-FU.
source: Following weekly injections of 5-FU, we documented that STAT1 KO mice died significantly faster than WT (p=0.01), and also faster than mice lacking both IFNAR and IFNGR (ARGR DKO) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The abundant HSCs observed in STAT1 KO spleen are more sensitive to depletion than WT stem cells, perhaps due to decreased quiescence or more rapid exhaustion following cycling.
source: Since the lethality of 5-FU is related to depletion of cycling stem and progenitor cells, this result suggests that the abundant HSCs observed in STAT1 KO spleen are more sensitive to depletion than WT stem cells, perhaps due to decreased quiescence or more rapid exhaustion following cycling.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased sensitivity to 5-FU treatment.

claim: The response of ARGR DKO animals to 5-FU challenge was indistinguishable (p=0.73) from WT animals.
source: Notably, the response of ARGR DKO animals to 5-FU challenge was indistinguishable (p=0.73) from WT animals, suggesting that IFN-I and IFN-II are not required to regulate HSC quiescence, at least in the presence of IFN-III.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: IFN-I and IFN-II are not required to regulate HSC quiescence, at least in the presence of IFN-III.
source: Notably, the response of ARGR DKO animals to 5-FU challenge was indistinguishable (p=0.73) from WT animals, suggesting that IFN-I and IFN-II are not required to regulate HSC quiescence, at least in the presence of IFN-III.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar response of ARGR DKO and WT mice to 5-FU.

claim: IFN-γ was increased approximately 300-fold in the sera of STAT1 KO animals (p<0.0001).
source: IFN-γ was increased approximately 300-fold in the sera of STAT1 KO animals and was moderately elevated in ARGR DKO mice (Figure 3A; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IFN-γ was moderately elevated in ARGR DKO mice.
source: IFN-γ was increased approximately 300-fold in the sera of STAT1 KO animals and was moderately elevated in ARGR DKO mice (Figure 3A; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IL-17A was found to average 100-fold higher concentration in STAT1 KO sera (p=0.04), with little or no elevation in ARGR DKO.
source: However, a more striking difference was noted for IL-17A, which was found to average 100-fold higher concentration in STAT1 KO sera (p=0.04), with little or no elevation in ARGR DKO (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The high concentrations of circulating IL-17A correlated with disease.
source: Since ARGR DKO animals, despite their lack of responsiveness to IFN-I and -II, showed little to no sign of pathology, the high concentrations of circulating IL-17A correlated with disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of IL-17A levels and disease phenotypes across genotypes.

claim: As many as 30% of STAT1-deficient CD4+ T cells produced IFN-γ (p=0.0061) as compared to only a few percent in WT controls.
source: We found that CD4+ T cells and NK cells were the main populations making IFN-γand IL-17A. As many as 30% of STAT1-deficient CD4+ T cells produced IFN-γ (p=0.0061) as compared to only a few percent in WT controls (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: A larger percentage of STAT1 KO CD4+ T and NK cells made IL-17A when compared to WT counterparts (p=0.0005).
source: Similarly, a larger percentage of STAT1 KO CD4+ T and NK cells made IL-17A when compared to WT counterparts (Figure 3D; p=0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The amount of IL-17A produced per cell was 5- to 10-fold greater in STAT1 KO cells, as indicated by increased mean fluorescence intensity (p<0.0004).
source: Moreover, not only was the number of IL-17 producing cells greater in STAT1 KO animals, but the amount of cytokine produced per cell was much greater, as indicated by a 5- to 10-fold increased mean fluorescence intensity (Figure 3E; p<0.0004).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The triple deficient strain that lacked IFN-I and IFN-II receptors (ARGR STAT1 TKO) still displayed the same altered parameters that were observed in mice singly deficient for STAT1.
source: The resulting triple deficient strain that lacked IFN-I and IFN-II receptors (ARGR STAT1 TKO) still displayed the same altered parameters that we observed in mice singly deficient for STAT1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alternate signals downstream of IFN receptors are unlikely culprits of the observed pathology in STAT1 KO mice.
source: Therefore, alternate signals downstream of IFN receptors are unlikely culprits of the observed pathology.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ARGR STAT1 TKO mice phenocopy STAT1 KO mice.

claim: Loss of IFN-I and II signaling (ARGR DKO) did not mimic the phenotype mediated by STAT1 loss.
source: However, loss of IFN-I and II signaling (ARGR DKO) did not mimic the phenotype mediated by STAT1 loss.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that ARGR DKO mice show mild phenotypes compared to STAT1 KO.

claim: ARGR DKO mice showed very mild signs of an altered immune system compared to STAT1 KO animals.
source: As previously noted, ARGR DKO mice showed very mild signs of an altered immune system compared to STAT1 KO animals.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of blood and spleen parameters.

claim: ARGR DKO mice did not present with splenomegaly and displayed very mild neutrophilia.
source: Despite being unresponsive to IFN-I and -II, these animals did not present with splenomegaly and displayed very mild neutrophilia (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ARGR DKO mice did not exhibit an increase of CD4+ effector T cells as observed in the STAT1 KO blood and spleen.
source: Interestingly, these animals did not exhibit an increase of CD4+ effector T cells as observed in the STAT1 KO blood and spleen (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: STAT2 KO animals showed profound defects that largely recapitulated what was observed in STAT1-deficient mice, except that no increase in the percentage of CD8+ effector T cells was detected in blood.
source: In contrast, STAT2 KO animals, which are impaired in their response to IFN-I and -III, showed profound defects that largely recapitulated what was observed in STAT1-deficient mice, except that no increase in the percentage of CD8+ effector T cells was detected in blood (Figure 4B-D).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: IFN-I and -III are the main cytokines acting through STAT1 to provide a protective environment to insure proper homeostasis of the immune system.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that IFN-I and -III are the main cytokines acting through STAT1 to provide a protective environment to insure proper homeostasis of the immune system, but additional STAT1-dependent functions are also at play.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes across different mutant strains.

claim: GR STAT2 DKO mice showed defects virtually identical to the ones observed for STAT1 KO mice.
source: Detailed flow cytometry analysis of the blood and spleen of GR STAT2 DKO mice uncovered defects virtually identical to the ones observed for STAT1 KO mice (Figure 4B and C), strongly indicating that the phenotype of STAT1- deficient mice is associated with combined insensitivity to IFN-I, -II, and -III (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The phenotype of STAT1-deficient mice is associated with combined insensitivity to IFN-I, -II, and -III.
source: Detailed flow cytometry analysis of the blood and spleen of GR STAT2 DKO mice uncovered defects virtually identical to the ones observed for STAT1 KO mice (Figure 4B and C), strongly indicating that the phenotype of STAT1- deficient mice is associated with combined insensitivity to IFN-I, -II, and -III (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarity between STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO mice.

claim: The number of splenic HSCs was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO (p=0.00007) and GR STAT2 DKO mice (p=0.026).
source: More importantly, the number of splenic HSCs was dramatically increased in STAT1 KO (p=0.00007) and GR STAT2 DKO mice (p=0.026), and this increase was not observed in the other mutant strains (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The combined absence of IFN-γR and STAT2 (GR STAT2 DKO) phenocopied STAT1 deficiency.
source: Taken together, our results strongly suggested that the combined absence of IFN-γR and STAT2 (GR STAT2 DKO) phenocopied STAT1 deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO mice.

claim: Both IFN-γ and IL-17A were elevated in GR STAT2 DKO mice compared to WT.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we measured IFN-γ and IL-17A production by CD4+ T cells and NK cells in these animals. Both cytokines were elevated compared to WT (Figure 4F and G), mimicking the phenotype of STAT1 KO cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: STAT1 KO mice developed spontaneous colitis, frequently accompanied by rectal prolapse.
source: In addition to the hematopoietic defects documented above, STAT1 KO mice developed spontaneous colitis, frequently accompanied by rectal prolapse.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by histological analysis.

claim: Gross anatomy of the STAT1-deficient colons revealed increased angiogenesis, a characteristic of inflamed bowels.
source: Gross anatomy of the STAT1-deficient colons revealed increased angiogenesis (Figure 5A), a characteristic of inflamed bowels (Alkim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by gross anatomical observations shown in Figure 5A and cited literature.

claim: Histopathologic analysis of colon sections documented extensive immune cell infiltrates, epithelial hyperplasia and goblet cell loss in STAT1 KO colons.
source: Histopathologic analysis of colon sections documented extensive im mune cell infiltrates, epithelial hyperplasia and goblet cell loss in STAT1 KO colons, associated in some cases with the presence of cryptitis (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Bacteria were observed mainly in the liver in STAT1 KO mice and to a lesser extent in the mesenteric lymph nodes and very rarely in the spleen.
source: Bacteria were observed mainly in the liver in STAT1 KO mice and to a lesser extent in the mesenteric lymph nodes and very rarely in the spleen (Figure 5D), while organs from WT animals were largely sterile.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial culture data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Signs of DSS-induced intestinal inflammation were more pronounced in STAT1-deficient mice than WT littermates.
source: In addition, we tested the sensitivity of STAT1 KO mice to dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis. Signs of DSS-induced intestinal inflammation, as evidenced by colon shortening and altered histopathology, were more pronounced in STAT1-deficient mice than WT littermates (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by DSS-induced colitis data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Analysis of alpha diversity revealed a significant reduction of bacterial taxa diversity in STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO animals compared to WT.
source: Analysis of alpha diversity measured by the Simpson and Shannon diversity indexes revealed a significant reduction of bacterial taxa diversity in STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO animals compared to WT, whereas the ARGR DKO microbiome was found to be as diverse as the controls (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The ARGR DKO microbiome was found to be as diverse as the controls.
source: Analysis of alpha diversity measured by the Simpson and Shannon diversity indexes revealed a significant reduction of bacterial taxa diversity in STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO animals compared to WT, whereas the ARGR DKO microbiome was found to be as diverse as the controls (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Commensal bacterial diversity was inversely correlated with the severity of the inflammatory disease.
source: Thus, commensal bacterial diversity was inversely correlated with the severity of the inflammatory disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mice with more severe disease had lower bacterial diversity.

claim: Analysis of the relative frequency of major bacterial families unveiled a large decrease of Bacteroidales S24-7 and Burkholderiales Alcaligenaceae in mutant strains.
source: Accordingly, analysis of the relative frequency of major bacterial families unveiled several significant differences between WT and mutant strains (Figure 6C), among them a large decrease of Bacteroidales S24-7 and Burkholderiales Alcaligenaceae and a consistent increase of Deferribacterales Deferribacteraceae and Campylobacterales Helicobacteraceae, suggesting that the abundance of these species is controlled by IFN (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Analysis of the relative frequency of major bacterial families unveiled a consistent increase of Deferribacterales Deferribacteraceae and Campylobacterales Helicobacteraceae in mutant strains.
source: Accordingly, analysis of the relative frequency of major bacterial families unveiled several significant differences between WT and mutant strains (Figure 6C), among them a large decrease of Bacteroidales S24-7 and Burkholderiales Alcaligenaceae and a consistent increase of Deferribacterales Deferribacteraceae and Campylobacterales Helicobacteraceae, suggesting that the abundance of these species is controlled by IFN (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The abundance of Bacteroidales S24-7, Burkholderiales Alcaligenaceae, Deferribacterales Deferribacteraceae, and Campylobacterales Helicobacteraceae is controlled by IFN.
source: Accordingly, analysis of the relative frequency of major bacterial families unveiled several significant differences between WT and mutant strains (Figure 6C), among them a large decrease of Bacteroidales S24-7 and Burkholderiales Alcaligenaceae and a consistent increase of Deferribacterales Deferribacteraceae and Campylobacterales Helicobacteraceae, suggesting that the abundance of these species is controlled by IFN (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential abundance of these species in IFN-deficient mice.

claim: Bacteroidales Prevotellaceae was increased only in STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO animals, correlating with disease severity.
source: However, another family, Bacteroidales Prevotellaceae, was of particular interest, since increases were present only in STAT1 KO and GR STAT2 DKO animals, therefore correlating with disease severity (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Two predominant clusters of amplicon sequence variants (ASV) related to the Prevotella family were increased in diseased animals.
source: Two predominant clusters of amplicon sequence variants (ASV) related to the Prevotella family were increased in diseased animals.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The ASV related to Prevotella clustered with Prevotella heparinolytica, a microbial species known to trigger TH17 responses.
source: This analysis revealed that these ASV clustered with Prevotella heparinolytica, a microbial species known to trigger TH17 responses (Calcinotto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and cited literature.

claim: ABX-treated STAT1 KO mice did not display splenomegaly (p=0.00011).
source: Strikingly, ABX-treated STAT1 KO mice did not display splenomegaly (Figure 6F; p=0.00011).
evidence: This is supported by spleen weight measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: ABX treatment restricted the accumulation of splenic CMP, GMP, and MEP progenitors as well as HSCs in STAT1 KO animals.
source: Moreover, ABX treatment restricted the accumulation of splenic CMP, GMP, and MEP progenitors as well as HSCs in STAT1 KO animals (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The elevated IL-17+ CD4+ T cells characteristic of STAT1 KO mice were significantly decreased by ABX treatment (p=0.0032).
source: Finally, peripheral blood leukocytes from ABX-treated and control STAT1 KO mice were examined for IL-17A production. The elevated IL-17+ CD4+ T cells characteristic of STAT1 KO mice were significantly decreased by ABX treatment (Figure 6H; p=0.0032).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: ABX-treated GR STAT2 DKO mice did not display splenomegaly, increased representation of myeloid cells in blood or accumulation of splenic progenitors.
source: Interestingly, reduction of microbial load through broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment showed a similar effect on GR STAT2 DKO mice. ABX-treated GR STAT2 DKO mice did not display splenomegaly, increased representation of myeloid cells in blood or accumulation of splenic progenitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: No difference in the generation of TH17 cells in vitro was observed between STAT1 KO and WT controls in response to IL-6 and TGF-β.
source: To examine mechanisms underlying the T cell alterations, we first probed the ability of STAT1 KO CD4+ T cells to differentiate into TH17 cells in vitro. No difference in the generation of TH17 cells in vitro was observed between STAT1 KO and WT controls in response to IL-6 and TGF-β (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro differentiation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant deficit was observed in production of STAT1 KO Treg compared to WT in vitro.
source: We next analyzed the capacity of STAT1 KO CD4+ T cells to differentiate into Treg cells in vitro in response to TGF-β and IL-2. Again, no significant deficit was observed in production of STAT1 KO Treg compared to WT (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro differentiation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Analysis of T cell populations in the thymus uncovered no statistically significant difference in thymic Treg populations (p=0.6 by Mann–Whitney).
source: Likewise, analysis of T cell populations in the thymus uncovered no statistically significant difference in thymic Treg populations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, p=0.6 by Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Peripheral Treg were virtually absent in STAT1 KO spleens.
source: However, contrasting with what we observed in vitro and in the thymus, peripheral Treg were virtually absent in STAT1 KO spleens (Figure 7A), consistent with colitis (Yamada et al., 2016) and with an inability to suppress TH17 expansion.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A and cited literature.

claim: Blocking IL-17 responses normalized the blood parameters of STAT1-deficient mice.
source: To directly test whether IL-17 could drive the anomalies observed in STAT1-deficient animals, we generated a mouse strain deficient for both Stat1 and Il17ra (STAT1 IL-17R DKO). Strikingly, blocking IL-17 responses normalized the blood parameters of STAT1-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by blood count data from STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice.

claim: STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice displayed at most a modest increase of the myeloid population.
source: An in-depth analysis of the representation of mature cells in the blood and spleen of these animals showed that STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice displayed at most a modest increase of the myeloid population (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C,E.

claim: Concomitant IL-17Ra deficiency lowered the percentage of GMPs observed in STAT1-deficient bone marrow and spleen, resolving this phenotype essentially to control levels.
source: Likewise, concomitant IL-17Ra deficiency lowered the percentage of GMPs observed in STAT1-deficient bone marrow and spleen, resolving this phenotype essentially to control levels (Figure 7D and F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7D,F.

claim: No increase of splenic HSCs was observed in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice.
source: More importantly, we observed no increase of splenic HSCs in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Accumulation of IFN-γ and IL-17A-producing CD4+ T cells and NK cells was not significantly different between STAT1 KO and STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice.
source: In contrast, accumulation of IFN-γ and IL-17A-producing CD4+ T cells and NK cells was not significantly different between STAT1 KO and STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Loss of IL-17 responsiveness reduced the abundance of IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-5, although all except IL-5 remained elevated compared to WT mice.
source: Analysis of plasma cytokine levels also showed increased abundance of inflammatory cytokines in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E). Interestingly, loss of IL-17 responsiveness reduced the abundance of IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-5, although all except IL-5 remained elevated compared to WT mice (p=0.003 for TNF-α; p=0.017 for IFN-γ).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: IL-17A appeared to be autoregulated, since its abundance was elevated in IL-17R KO mice (p=0.0022) and even higher in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice (p=0.0028).
source: IL-17A appeared to be autoregulated, since its abundance was elevated in IL-17R KO mice (p=0.0022) and even higher in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E, p=0.0028).
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated IL-17A levels in IL-17R-deficient mice.

claim: Effector T lymphocyte and cytokine levels remained elevated in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice, suggesting that they are primary responses to the lack of STAT1 signaling rather than to elevated IL-17A.
source: That effector T lymphocyte and cytokine levels remained elevated in STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice, in spite of the resolution of the myeloproliferative phenotype, suggests that they are primary responses to the lack of STAT1 signaling rather than to elevated IL-17A.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of elevated cytokines despite blocking IL-17 signaling.

claim: Microbial dysbiosis was still present in STAT1 IL-17R DKO animals, similar to what was previously observed for STAT1 and GR STAT2 KO mice.
source: Because we hypothesized that microbial dysbiosis is the primary trigger of inflammation in STAT1 KO mice, we examined gut microbial diversity of STAT1 IL-17R DKO mice. Microbial dysbiosis was still present in STAT1 IL-17R DKO animals, similar to what was previously observed for STAT1 and GR STAT2 KO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Increased IL-17A signaling is the primary driver of the myeloproliferative phenotype in STAT1 KO animals but is secondary to microbial dysbiosis, alterations in lymphocyte subsets, and other inflammatory cytokines.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that increased IL-17A signaling is the primary driver of the myeloproliferative phenotype in STAT1 KO animals but is secondary to microbial dysbiosis, alterations in lymphocyte subsets, and other inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking IL-17 resolves myeloproliferation but not dysbiosis or other inflammatory markers.

claim: Tonic signaling through the IFN pathway, acting through its common mediator STAT1, is an essential modulator of immune homeostasis, reducing the propensity for inflammation.
source: Our data provide evidence that tonic signaling through the IFN pathway, acting through its common mediator STAT1, is an essential modulator of immune homeostasis, reducing the propensity for inflammation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: The absence of tonic IFN signaling allows development of a skewed microbiome that triggers an inflammatory response.
source: The absence of tonic IFN signaling allows development of a skewed microbiome that triggers an inflammatory response, likely due to an increased bias of TH17 cells toward a pathogenic phenotype and impaired homing or survival of peripheral Treg.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of dysbiosis and inflammatory disease in STAT1 KO mice.

claim: IL-17 has been shown to stimulate myeloid and erythroid progenitors.
source: Interestingly, besides its important role in inflammation, IL-17 also plays a significant role in hematopoiesis (Krstic et al., 2012). For instance, IL-17 stimulates myeloid and erythroid progenitors (Lubberts et al., 2001; Krstic et al., 2010), suggesting that IFN-III could play a role in the regulation of hematopoiesis through limiting the action of IL-17.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Human STAT1 deficiency results in increased susceptibility to both viral and mycobacterial infections.
source: As expected, human STAT1 deficiency results in increased susceptibility to both viral and mycobacterial infections (Dupuis et al., 2001; Dupuis et al., 2003), and hematopoietic cell transplantation remains the only curative treatment (Bustamante et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on human STAT1 deficiency.

claim: Some STAT1 partial loss of function (LOF) patients suffer from chronic colitis, as well as severe infections.
source: However, some STAT1 partial loss of function (LOF) patients suffer from chronic colitis, as well as severe infections (Thoeni et al., 2015; Sharfe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on human STAT1 LOF patients.

claim: Individuals with STAT1 gain-of-function (GOF) mutations suffer most frequently from mucocutaneous diseases, in part due to depressed levels of TH17 cells.
source: On the other hand, individuals with STAT1 gain-of-function (GOF) mutations suffer most frequently from mucocutaneous diseases, in part due to depressed levels of TH17 cells, thereby attributing important regulatory functions to STAT1 (Liu et al., 2011; Puel, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on human STAT1 GOF mutations.

claim: IFN-III has been shown to resolve inflammation by reducing the number of IL-17-producing TH17 helper T cells and restricting the recruitment of neutrophils.
source: For instance, IFN-III has been shown to resolve inflammation by reducing the number of IL-17-producing TH17 helper T cells and restricting the recruitment of neutrophils (Blazek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: IFN-III members display a unique capacity to counter pathogen invasion at mucosal sites while curbing overexuberant inflammation that helps maintain barrier integrity.
source: Moreover, in part because of the more limited distribution of their receptor, IFN-III members display a unique capacity to counter pathogen invasion at mucosal sites while curbing overexuberant inflammation that helps maintain barrier integrity (Pott and Stockinger, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Commensal gut microbiota play fundamental roles in shaping the host immune system.
source: There is mounting evidence that commensal gut microbiota that exist at mucosal surfaces also play fundamental roles in shaping the host immune system (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Gutierrez-Merino et al., 2020; Castillo-Álvarez et al., 2018; Alteber et al., 2018; Canesso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A distinct strain of STAT1 KO mice (Balb/c) housed in an independent animal facility was previously reported to develop a myeloid proliferative disease accompanied by progenitor expansion.
source: Myeloid hyperplasia in the absence of STAT1 is not unprecedented, since a distinct strain of STAT1 KO mice (Balb/c) housed in an independent animal facility was previously reported to develop a myeloid proliferative disease accompanied by progenitor expansion (Porpaczy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: IL-17 has been shown to stimulate granulopoiesis and the recruitment of both short- and long-term stem cells.
source: For instance, IL-17 has been shown to stimulate myeloid progenitors and early-stage erythroid progenitors. Overexpression or exogenous administration of IL-17 stimulates granulopoiesis and the recruitment of both short- and long-term stem cells (Lubberts et al., 2001), relocating core erythropoiesis from bone marrow to spleen (Krstic et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: STAT1 acts at an early stage of TH17 differentiation to impair pathogenesis.
source: Consistent with our data, it has been suggested that STAT1 acts at an early stage of TH17 differentiation to impair pathogenesis (Yosef et al., 2013), although its molecular targets and the mechanisms regulating TH17 pathogenic potential remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A role for the gut microbiome in regulating the response to systemic type I IFN has been documented.
source: A role for the gut microbiome in regulating the response to systemic type I IFN has been documented (Bradley et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2012; Ganal et al., 2012; Steed et al., 2017; Ito et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Commensal microbiota are the major regulator of steady state IFN production.
source: Recent studies have also substantiated the role of commensal microbiota as the major regulator of steady state IFN production (Gutierrez-Merino et al., 2020; McAleer and Kolls, 2012; Abt et al., 2012), for example by identifying microbiota-controlled tonic IFN expression by pDCs to be instrumental to 'instruct' responsiveness of cDCs, poising them for future immune intervention (Schaupp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Microbiota dysbiosis has been associated with human diseases where the IFN system is perturbed, such as systemic lupus erythematosus.
source: Interestingly, microbiota dysbiosis has also been associated with human diseases where the IFN system is perturbed, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (Silverman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Bacteroidales S24-7 has been described as a beneficial commensal in a mouse model of preclinical inflammatory arthritis.
source: We found that the gut microbiota of STAT1-deficient mice is depleted of Bacteroidales S24-7, which has been described as a beneficial commensal in a mouse model of preclinical inflammatory arthritis (Rogier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A number of Prevotella sp., including P. copri, P. bivia, P. heparinolytica, P. nigrescens, and P. intermedia, has been found to drive inflammation through induction of IL-17.
source: Of note, a number of Prevotella sp., including P. copri, P. bivia, P. heparinolytica, P. nigrescens, and P. intermedia, has been found to drive inflammation through induction of IL-17.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Prevotella sp. have been tied to a number of human chronic inflammatory diseases, such as new-onset rheumatoid arthritis (NORA), periodontitis, asthma, and bacterial vaginosis.
source: Prevotella sp. have also been tied to a number of human chronic inflammatory diseases, such as new-onset rheumatoid arthritis (NORA), periodontitis, asthma, and bacterial vaginosis (Scher et al., 2013; Larsen, 2017; Si et al., 2017; Lopes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Many genes associated with IBD susceptibility are related to the IFN pathway.
source: The susceptibility of STAT1 KO mice to development of IBD is consistent with the observation that human patients carrying a hypomorphic allele of STAT1 develop symptoms of colitis (Thoeni et al., 2015; Sharfe et al., 2014) and that many genes associated with IBD susceptibility are related to the IFN pathway (Jostins et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: STAT1 functions as a tumor suppressor through multiple mechanisms.
source: For instance, STAT1 functions as a tumor suppressor through multiple mechanisms (Meissl et al., 2017) prevention of inflammation through modulation of the microbiota may provide another facet of its barrier to tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.
